Stories / London · Norway · Denmark · 1814

Story · Norwegian independence, 19th century

London, 1814: a crown for Norway, a princess for its king

On 17 May 1814, at Eidsvoll, Norway gives itself a constitution and elects the Danish prince Christian Frederik as its king. No great power recognises it: by the Treaty of Kiel, Denmark has ceded Norway to Sweden. In London the new king’s envoy, Carsten Anker, seeks British support. On 28 June he slips a partly enciphered leaf into his mail: Princess Charlotte, heiress to the British throne, has just broken off her engagement. The king must not commit himself elsewhere.

Story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · document: Arkivverket, Riksarkivet (Oslo), RA-EA-5938 Christian Frederik · published 14 November 2026

« Kun at D.K.H. ei binder sig! »

“If only Your Royal Highness does not bind yourself!”: Carsten Anker to Christian Frederik, London, 28 June 1814 (cipher passage, royal sign restored).

What is new, what was known

Known. The 1814 correspondence of Christian Frederik and Carsten Anker was printed in Christiania by C. J. Anker, with the cipher passages of the main dispatches given in clear; it is online at the Royal Danish Library.[2] The prince’s letters there mention the plan of a marriage with Princess Charlotte of Wales. The Oslo archives also hold the keys and the contemporary decipherment of a cipher letter by Anker of 1811.[1]

What we add, to our knowledge. (1) The reading of the leaf “fr. 28 Junii 1814”, half cipher, half clear, which the edition does not print and which carries no gloss: read, 249 of 252 cipher signs (98.8%). (2) The key of Anker’s 1811 cipher, rebuilt from the contemporary decipherment and tested on a held-out portion. (3) Anker’s answer to the prince’s plan, known until now only from Christian Frederik’s side.

1814: a kingdom nobody recognises

Christian Frederik, cousin and heir presumptive of King Frederick VI of Denmark-Norway, has governed Norway since 1813. On 14 January 1814, by the Treaty of Kiel, defeated Denmark cedes Norway to the King of Sweden. The Norwegians refuse; the prince is elected regent in February, then king on 17 May, after the constitution is adopted at Eidsvoll, in Carsten Anker’s manor.[3] A businessman and close adviser of the prince, Anker had represented the Danish Asia Company in London from 1805; he returns there in March 1814 to plead Norway’s cause, and achieves little.[4] The prince has no wife: he divorced in 1810.[3]

A marriage idea

In London, on 10 June 1814, Princess Charlotte of Wales, only daughter of the Prince Regent and heiress to the throne, signs her marriage contract with the Hereditary Prince of Orange; soon after, failing agreement on her conditions, she breaks it off.[5] On 24 June, not yet knowing this, Christian Frederik writes to Anker: should the Storting turn to England, “the intended connection with Princess Charlotte” would be “doubly important”; “Norway could then become an independent kingdom in union with Great Britain”.[2]

On 28 June Anker sends him the leaf. The sensitive words are in cipher:

“The match [of the princess] with the Prince of Orange is broken off pour jamais. Now my old idée rises again: the princess is handsome, she has a very firm character, she must absolutely marry. She will not be allowed to leave the country, and one would have to accept that. […] In eight to fourteen days Your Royal Highness’s portrait will be ready, well engraved and published. […] If only Your Royal Highness does not bind yourself! […] Hardenberg and I have talked about it a great deal, and we agree.”

Between the cipher passages, the clear text says the rest: were the prince not bound and “Norway’s horizon” to brighten, the idea would deserve weighing; the country’s lasting happiness would be all but secured. The leaf shows that the idea was Anker’s (“my old idea”) and that he was pursuing it in London with a Hardenberg whom the letter does not specify.

The end of a dream

The dream is short-lived. In July Sweden attacks; the Convention of Moss, on 14 August, ends the war, and Christian Frederik hands power to the Storting and abdicates; on 4 November the Storting elects the King of Sweden.[3] On 12 December, back in Denmark, the prince writes to Anker that he needed his news about Princess Charlotte quickly, “otherwise the Augustenborg matter will be settled”; on 22 May 1815 he marries his cousin Caroline Amalie of Augustenborg.[2] Charlotte marries Leopold of Saxe-Coburg in 1816 and dies the following year.[5]

The leaf of 28 June catches the moment when, for a few weeks, two men imagined making independent Norway a kingdom tied to Great Britain by a marriage.

The leaf’s record →

The leaf of 28 June 1814

Danish text, spelling of the manuscript. In bold, the cipher put into clear; {x} probable; [x] restored; ‹…› unresolved; in italics, the manuscript’s clear text.

Parti{e}s med Pr: af {O}ranien er afbr{u}dt pour jamais. N{u} opstaaer min gamle Idée : Prindcesen er sm{u}k, har en megen fast Care{k}ter, skal absol{u}t giftes. — {U}d af Landet faaer h{u}n ikke Lov at gaae, og det maatte man finde sig i. — Var nu [D.K.H.] ei b{u}nden‹?› og oplystedes Norriges Horizont saa var Idéen vel værd at overtænke. — Grunden og selve Bygningen til N. stadige Lykke, Roe og Velstand var da med et lagt og mesten færdig. Om 8 à 14 Dage bliver [D.K.H.]s Portrait færdigt, godt st{u}kket og p{u}bliceret. Men dette er en vidtløftig Materie, som kræver Tid. K{u}n at [D.K.H.] ei binder sig! Gud veed, at ingen kan ivrigere end jeg ønske D. K. H.s sande Lyksalighed. Min hulde ædle og elskede Herre! At De høre deem ikke ‹felv› til. Hardenberg og jeg have meget talt herom og vi ere eenige.

Translation: “The match with the Prince of Orange is broken off for ever. Now my old idea rises again: the princess is handsome, she has a very firm character, she must absolutely marry. She will not be allowed to leave the country, and one would have to accept that. Were Your Royal Highness not bound, and Norway’s horizon to brighten, the idea would well deserve weighing: the foundations and the very building of Norway’s lasting happiness, peace and prosperity would then be laid at a stroke and almost finished. In eight to fourteen days Your Royal Highness’s portrait will be ready, well engraved and published. But this is a wide matter, which needs time. If only Your Royal Highness does not bind yourself! God knows that no one can wish more ardently than I the true happiness of Your Royal Highness. My gracious, noble and beloved master! That you do not belong to them [‹felv›, sense uncertain]. Hardenberg and I have talked about it a great deal, and we agree.”

The cipher

  • Symbols: an alphabet of invented signs, with homophones (three signs for a, two for e, g, m and o).
  • A logogram for “Deres Kongelige Høihed”, Your Royal Highness, restored from the sense (three occurrences).
  • Mixed clear text: Danish and French alternate with the cipher, word by word.

The archival file holds at least three symbol alphabets, a numerical cipher alphabet, several three- and four-figure codebooks and four perforated grilles. The 1814 leaf follows the alphabet of the 1811 letter, not the one dated Bergen, 22 March 1814, although that one too has a logogram for “Deres Kongelige Høihed”.

How we read it

  1. A declared first failure. A pencil key sheet of modern appearance, found in the file, was tested under a protocol written and hashed in advance: 0.025 of characters right, barely above the controls. It is only a partial reconstruction; we set it aside.
  2. A rebuilt and validated key. A new key, learnt from the glossed page of the 1811 letter, frozen, then applied to another column of the same letter, transcribed and frozen before any comparison with its contemporary decipherment: 0.950 of characters right, against at best 0.019 for 200 control keys.
  3. The right alphabet. Before reading, the 1814 leaf was compared with the file’s alphabets: it follows the 1811 one (0.937 against 0.369 for the Bergen alphabet).
  4. The reading, sign by sign, counted by Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: sure, probable (four new forms fixed by several concordant words), restored not counted.

What remains uncertain

  • A short text. 252 cipher signs: 249 sure or probable (98.8%); the royal logogram, restored three times, is not counted. One word remains of uncertain sense.
  • Hardenberg is not identified: the name was enough for the letter, not for us.
  • A transcription by a single reader, from the images; no second blind reader for this leaf.
  • Prior work. Checked on 14 November 2026: C. J. Anker’s edition (full-text search of 254 letters), Daniel Bourdeau’s repository, web search. We found no study of the Charlotte plan; Norwegian and Danish studies of 1814 were not consulted.
  • No images. Arkivverket’s images can be downloaded freely, but no reuse licence is displayed; they are not reproduced here.
